analysis.one_liner: Sends every eligible adult a $12,000 refundable tax rebate, phasing out above middle incomes.
analysis.headline: A bill for a fourth round of stimulus checks — $12,000 per person — never got a hearing or a vote, dying in committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a fourth round of COVID-style stimulus checks: a fully refundable $12,000 tax credit for every eligible adult ($24,000 for married couples) for tax year 2022, with the amount shrinking for single filers earning above $75,000 and couples above $150,000. The payment could not be seized by creditors or garnished, and the IRS would have run outreach to reach people who don't file tax returns. It never left the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, most Americans would receive a $12,000 payment ($24,000 per couple) in late 2022, regardless of whether they owed income tax. The full amount would go to single filers making under $75,000 and couples under $150,000, phasing out quickly above that. Payments would be shielded from federal offsets, most private garnishment, and bankruptcy proceedings, and the IRS would have to actively help non-filers claim the money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nearly all taxpayers, especially lower-income households

how_it_helps.text: Gives every eligible individual a fully refundable $12,000 credit ($24,000 per married couple) for tax year 2022, meaning even people who owe no income tax receive the full amount as a payment.
Full payment for single filers with modified adjusted gross income up to $75,000 ($150,000 joint), phasing out over a narrow band above that.
Payments would be exempt from federal offsets and from garnishment by creditors, with protections letting account holders shield the money from bank garnishment orders.
Requires an IRS outreach program to help people who do not normally file tax returns claim the payment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would have paid out roughly $2.5 trillion or more, funded by borrowing, a cost ultimately borne by taxpayers and future budgets. Because payments would be exempt from garnishment and offsets, creditors and government agencies collecting debts could not touch the money.

drawbacks.text: A $12,000-per-person payment to most Americans would cost the federal government trillions of dollars, adding to the national debt and potentially fueling inflation, which was high in 2022 and falls hardest on people with the lowest incomes.

The income phase-out is abrupt: a single filer loses the entire $12,000 once modified adjusted gross income reaches $80,000, so a worker just above that line gets nothing while someone earning slightly less gets the full amount.

Payments made in advance to non-filers are calculated without applying the income limit unless the government has reason to know it applies, which could direct payments to higher-income people who did not file.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a large, immediate cash payment to most households — would have been substantial but extremely expensive, funded by federal borrowing, and many economists would argue that by 2022 such a payment risked adding to inflation rather than relieving it. The bill also had no way forward: it never had a cosponsor or committee action, so its design was never seriously examined or improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2022, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 3, 2022 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The only recorded actions are introduction and referral; there was no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No identifiable interest fought for or against it; the outcome simply leaves the tax code unchanged. Low-income households lost a potential payment, while the federal government avoided an estimated cost in the trillions and creditors kept their ability to garnish.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one in particular; the bill simply expired

for.name: Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No one else in either party cosponsored the bill and no votes were taken, so no partisan divide was ever visible.

industries.note: The bill requires banks to run garnishment procedures on stimulus payments and shields account holders' stimulus funds from certain garnishment orders, while protecting compliant banks from liability. A one-time administrative cost, no revenue effect.

Because stimulus payments would be exempt from garnishment, attachment, and offset, creditors could not seize them to satisfy debts. Most such creditors are companies and individuals owed money by low-income debtors.
